name: Observable
first: A class whose stored properties report each read and each change, so that SwiftUI runs again the body of each view that read a property that changed.

dependsOn.why: An observable type is a class, so every view that uses one instance sees the same values.
dependsOn.whyInExample: The type `Trip` is a class, as `Counter` is, and `NightsLabel` holds a reference to the one `trip`.

dependsOn.why: A class becomes observable through a macro, which adds the code that reports each read and each change.
dependsOn.whyInExample: The attribute `@Observable` is an attached macro, as `#function` on the page of Macro is a freestanding one.

dependsOn.why: SwiftUI runs a body again only when a value that the body read changes, and an observable class reports which of its properties a body read.
dependsOn.whyInExample: The body of `NightsLabel` reads `trip.nights`, as the body of `Counter` on the page of View update reads `taps`.

sil.shows: The macro makes nights a computed property, whose getter reports each read by calling access(keyPath:) with a key path to nights.
The getter reads the value from _nights, a stored property that the macro adds.
The setter reports each change by calling withMutation(keyPath:_:), which makes the change.

what.is: An observable class is a class marked with the macro `@Observable`. The macro makes each stored property report when code reads it and when code changes it. SwiftUI notes which properties each view's `body` read, and when one of those properties changes, it runs that `body` again.
what.afterExample: The `body` of `NightsLabel` reads `nights`, and never reads `city`. So line 21, which changes `city`, runs no `body`, and line 23, which changes `nights`, runs it again.
what.problem: Data that several views share, such as a trip that a list and an editor both show, cannot be state, because state belongs to one view. A class can be shared, but SwiftUI has no way to see a change to a plain class. An observable class reports its changes, and SwiftUI updates only the views that read what changed.
what.how: The macro turns each stored property into a computed property, and keeps the value in a stored property of its own. Its getter reports the read, with a key path to the property, and its setter reports the change. While SwiftUI runs a `body`, it collects the reads. When a property it collected changes, it runs that `body` again.

when.text: Use it for the data of an app that several views read and change, such as a store of trips, on iOS 17 or later.
Don't use it for a value that only one view uses, such as whether a menu is open. A state property is simpler.

parts.name: The macro `@Observable`, line 3
parts.text: An attached macro written before the class. When swiftc builds the program, it adds code to `Trip`: a stored property that keeps the value of each property, and code that reports each read and each change.

parts.name: The tracked properties, lines 5 and 6
parts.text: The properties `nights` and `city` are written as plain stored properties. The macro makes each one a computed property that reports each read and each change, and keeps its value in a stored property that the macro adds.

parts.name: The read of `trip.nights`, line 12
parts.text: The `body` of `NightsLabel` reads `nights` on lines 12 and 13. Each read reports itself, so SwiftUI notes that this `body` depends on `nights` of this trip, and not on `city`.

steps.text: Line 17 makes a `Trip`, and line 18 makes a `NightsLabel` that holds a reference to it. Line 19 makes a renderer for the label.
Line 20 asks for the image, so SwiftUI runs the `body` of `NightsLabel`. Line 12 reads `trip.nights`, which reports the read, and prints {{body runs: 3}}.

Line 21 changes `city`, which reports the change. No `body` read `city`, so SwiftUI has nothing to update. Line 22 runs the main run loop, the loop that does the work waiting on the main thread, for a tenth of a second, and no `body` runs.
Line 23 changes `nights` to 5. The `body` of `NightsLabel` read `nights`, so SwiftUI marks that view to update.
Line 24 runs the main run loop, where SwiftUI does its waiting updates. It runs the `body` again, and line 12 prints {{body runs: 5}}.

end.text: The class reported each read and each change. SwiftUI ran the `body` again for the change to `nights`, which it read, and not for `city`.
